history.heading: Norse settlement
paragraphs: The Faroe Islands, 18 rugged islands in the North Atlantic between Norway, Iceland and Scotland, may have been visited by Irish monks before Norse settlers arrived in the 9th century. The settlers established the Løgting, one of the oldest parliaments in the world, in Tórshavn.
The islands came under Norwegian rule and, with Norway, under Denmark from 1380. When Norway was separated from Denmark in 1814, the Faroes remained Danish.

history.heading: Toward self-government
paragraphs: A national movement in the 19th century promoted the Faroese language. During the Second World War, Britain occupied the islands after Germany invaded Denmark. A 1946 independence referendum narrowly favoured independence, but the result was disputed, and in 1948 the Faroes received home rule within the Danish realm.

culture.heading: Language and traditions
paragraphs: Faroese, a North Germanic language descended from Old Norse, is the main language; Danish is also used. Most people belong to the Faroese Lutheran church.

The traditional chain dance, accompanied by long ballads (kvæði), is still performed. Faroese cuisine includes fermented and dried lamb (ræst kjøt), fish and seabirds. The traditional pilot whale hunt (grindadráp) is culturally important locally but controversial internationally.

politics.heading: Self-governing nation
paragraphs: The Faroe Islands are a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark with their own parliament, the Løgting, and government led by a prime minister. They handle most domestic affairs, while Denmark is responsible for defence and some foreign policy matters.
The Faroes are not part of the European Union. Some parties favour full independence, and the islands elect two members to the Danish parliament.

economy.heading: Fishing nation
paragraphs: Fishing and aquaculture, especially farmed salmon, account for the vast majority of exports, making the Faroes highly prosperous. Tourism has grown, attracted by dramatic cliffs and landscapes. Undersea road tunnels link many islands.
The currency is the Faroese króna, equal in value to the Danish krone.
